text:
MENA startups raised $40 million in October. In September they raised $1.1 billion.

That is the headline from Wamda and Digital Digest's monthly report, published this week. A 96% drop in one month. But the detail matters more than the headline.

What the numbers say:

1. No megadeals at all. September was lifted by three large Saudi fintech rounds. October had none, so the total collapsed.
2. Deals fell far less than dollars. Deal count went from 73 to 32 (down 56%). Investors are still writing cheques, just smaller ones.
3. B2B took about 86% of the money. Early-stage rounds took more than 84%.
4. Saudi Arabia led with $18.8 million across nine startups. The UAE followed with $12.9 million across ten.

Our read: capital in the region is getting selective. When the big cheques pause, investors and boards ask harder questions. Does the technology actually work? Can the team run it in production? Is the valuation grounded in real revenue?

That is where technical due diligence earns its place. In a tighter market, the companies that can show working systems, not demos, are the ones that raise.

text:
34120 Consultants, UAE/GCC Capital Markets Morning Update

Friday, 13 November 2026

FAB's proposed AED 15bn rights issue is the story of the week. The board priced it at AED 13.52 a share, a 30% discount to Tuesday's close, and the stock closed 9.64% higher on Thursday on AED 829m of turnover, more than three times its average. That carried the ADX General Index up 1.47% to 9,725.72. Mubadala, which holds 37.9%, intends to take its full entitlement. Shareholders vote on 7 December and the raise is expected to complete in Q1 2027.

What makes it more than a bank topping up capital is where the money is aimed. FAB has guided to 10-15% annual loan and revenue growth through 2031 and named technology and AI among the capabilities it is funding.

Two other announcements this week point the same way. Blackstone opened a Private Wealth office in DIFC, its second UAE location after Abu Dhabi, sitting on more than 40 distributor relationships across the region. And Emirates NBD signed an MoU with J.P. Morgan Asset Management to explore distributing active ETFs through its digital wealth architecture, days after switching on AI-generated market insights on ENBD X built with Bridgewise.

34120 view: global managers are putting permanent people and infrastructure on the ground here, not just capital flowing through. That is the part worth paying attention to, because it is the part that needs local commercial talent.

Source: ADX, Reuters, FAB, Blackstone, Emirates NBD, Bridgewise.

author: Jean Abillama, CFA
headline: Investment Management | ex-PIMCO | HBS | US <​> MENA
text:
Gulf sovereign wealth is usually discussed as one block of capital heading west. PwC's new study of the world's 350 largest state investors, published today, shows it splitting in two.

Qatar Investment Authority has pledged $500 billion of US investment over a decade. MGX, Abu Dhabi's AI vehicle, aims to deploy roughly 80% of its investments in the United States, and ADQ's and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA)'s bets on power and data centres are centred on America. The rationale is plain in the report: access to US technology, AI and semiconductors.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is going the other way. From a foreign allocation that peaked near 30%, it is cutting toward 18 to 20%, redirecting capital to Vision 2030 projects and sovereign AI at home, and imposing spending discipline across the portfolio.

For a US manager or company active in the region, this changes which conversation to have. In Doha and Abu Dhabi the question is how a deal deepens access to American technology. In Riyadh it is increasingly what the deal builds inside the Kingdom. Capital that used to be marketed to as a single GCC bundle now has to be read fund by fund.

text:
Goldman Sachs , HSBC , and Fortress Investment Group just teamed up with regional managers Ruya Partners and Amwal Capital Partners Capital Partners to back a $150 million private credit facility for United Saudi Company  

On the surface, it looks like another cross-border financing deal in the Kingdom. Dig a little deeper, and it signals a much bigger shift in how GCC capital markets are evolving.

As regional tensions and tighter financial conditions strain traditional Saudi banks, alternative non-bank lenders are stepping in to fill the funding gap. Further, this private credit growth directly supports Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s economic diversification push by keeping capital flowing to local manufacturers. Here are three takeaways worth watching:

1️⃣ 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗹𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗴𝗮𝗽: Traditional Saudi banks have been stretched by massive Vision 2030 infrastructure and corporate capex demands. Alternative lenders are stepping directly into that white space to offer speed and flexible structuring where conventional balance sheets are tightening.

2️⃣ 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝗶𝗮𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗲: Notice the syndicate structure. Global heavyweight capital from Goldman and Fortress didn't go it alone - they partnered alongside regional players like Ruya and Amwal. In the GCC, regulatory fluency and local origination relationships remain the real moat.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) is going the other way. From a foreign allocation that peaked near 30%, it is cutting toward 18 to 20%, redirecting capital to Vision 2030 projects and sovereign AI at home, and imposing spending discipline across the portfolio.

For a US manager or company active in the region, this changes which conversation to have. In Doha and Abu Dhabi the question is how a deal deepens access to American technology. In Riyadh it is increasingly what the deal builds inside the Kingdom. Capital that used to be marketed to as a single GCC bundle now has to be read fund by fund.

Saudi property prices rose 1.2% last quarter. The average is the least interesting number in the release.

GASTAT's Q3 2026 Real Estate Price Index came in at 105.1 points, up 1.2% year-on-year but down 1.2% against Q2. Underneath that headline:

- Residential +2.3% y/y, commercial -2.0%
- Residential land +4.9%, apartments +1.7%, villas -7.7%
- Riyadh +4.6%, Northern Borders +12%, Madinah +0.3%

Financing moved the other way. SAMA data puts new residential mortgage lending by banks at roughly SAR 17.3 billion in Q3, up 5.3% from SAR 16.4 billion in Q2, though September alone softened to SAR 5.5 billion across about 9,700 contracts.

Land up almost 5% while finished villas fall nearly 8% is the spread worth underwriting against. It squeezes the developer margin from both ends: entry cost climbing, exit price easing. Capital is still committing anyway. Reportage Saudi Arabia announced SAR 1.1 billion this week for two townhouse projects in Al Arid, 148 units combined.

If your villa exit assumptions were set in 2025, when did you last re-run them?

text:
MENA startups raised $40 million in October. In September they raised $1.1 billion.

That is the headline from Wamda and Digital Digest's monthly report, published this week. A 96% drop in one month. But the detail matters more than the headline.

What the numbers say:

1. No megadeals at all. September was lifted by three large Saudi fintech rounds. October had none, so the total collapsed.
2. Deals fell far less than dollars. Deal count went from 73 to 32 (down 56%). Investors are still writing cheques, just smaller ones.
3. B2B took about 86% of the money. Early-stage rounds took more than 84%.
4. Saudi Arabia led with $18.8 million across nine startups. The UAE followed with $12.9 million across ten.

Our read: capital in the region is getting selective. When the big cheques pause, investors and boards ask harder questions. Does the technology actually work? Can the team run it in production? Is the valuation grounded in real revenue?

That is where technical due diligence earns its place. In a tighter market, the companies that can show working systems, not demos, are the ones that raise.

Raqi.ai helps GCC investors and businesses with technical due diligence, valuation and private, bilingual Arabic and English AI.

When this region was tested this year, real estate did what it’s supposed to do. It held.

Dubai residential prices softened 4 to 7% between February and April. Listed real estate stocks fell 34% at their peak. Same city, same asset class, very different outcomes.

That’s why family offices and investment holdings here lean on property. Middle East family offices hold around 15% of their portfolios in real estate, against 10% globally.

But “it held” is an average. And averages are where decisions go to hide.

Depending on location, mainstream prices fell anywhere from 5% to 20%. Two investors could own property in the same city, through the same crisis, and have completely different years.

Now scale that up. A family holding with villas in Dubai, off-plan units in Abu Dhabi and a commercial position in Riyadh. Each market reports differently. Different data access, different definitions, different lag. There is still no common GCC benchmark to put them side by side.

So the most important question, “where should our next dirham go?”, is often answered with broker calls, a few PDFs and gut feel.

International trade is built on movement. Ships move cargo. Capital moves across borders. Businesses move into new markets...And disputes? They have an extraordinary ability to travel even further...

A shipping disagreement can become a cross-border commercial battle. An oil and gas transaction can turn into a governance challenge. A private equity deal can suddenly involve arbitration, regulatory questions and several jurisdictions.

In other words, the business may have one transaction. The lawyers may have five countries, three legal systems and a very long week ahead!

That's why we're delighted to welcome Chehade Kahi, Founder of Montmartre & Co Legal Consultancies, UAE, to GLA MENA 2026.

With over 20 years of experience across the GCC and wider Middle East, Chehade brings expertise in shipping, international trade, oil and gas, private equity, M&A and complex corporate matters. He has also served as General Counsel and Board Secretary at Emirates Petroleum Company, and as an arbitrator before the Dubai Chamber of Commerce, with appointments in disputes before SIAC.

He's also a keen voice on legal innovation and artificial intelligence, because even the legal profession can't keep navigating the future with yesterday's compass!

Egypt ranks as the third-largest market in Endeavor Catalyst's global investment portfolio, and the firm plans to deepen its presence in the country. 

The venture capital investment arm of Endeavor intends to deploy USD 15 million to USD 20 million in Egypt through its fifth fund, backing between 8 and 10 startups over the next four years. 

The fund recently closed at USD 320 million, bringing Endeavor Catalyst's total assets under management to more than USD 850 million. 

Globally, it aims to invest in 150 companies across 50 countries, with individual investments typically ranging from USD 1 million to USD 3 million. 

For Egypt's startup ecosystem, the planned allocation adds another source of institutional venture capital targeting fast-growing technology companies.
